title: Not Just the Lining
subtitle: A blocked nose that a spray cannot fix, from the first visit to the splints coming out
description: Taking a history that separates lining from structure, the Cottle maneuver, confirming the deviation on endoscopy, choosing the graft, protecting the inferior turbinate, closing without packing, and why a caudal septum comes back when it is not fixed to the spine.

steps.title: Step 1/7: The History
steps.scenario:
A 50-year-old man comes to clinic with years of nasal obstruction. You take the history before you touch him.

The block is on the left, it is there every day, and it does not move from side to side. He used an intranasal corticosteroid correctly for four months on his family doctor's advice and noticed almost no change. He also gets a watery nose some mornings. No facial pressure, no loss of smell.
steps.question: Which feature of the history points to a fixed structural cause rather than swollen lining?

options.text: (A) The watery rhinorrhea in the mornings
(B) A constant block on one side that does not switch sides and did not change after four months of a correctly used steroid spray
(C) Symptoms lasting for years
(D) The absence of facial pressure

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

Swollen lining behaves in a recognizable way. It follows the nasal cycle, so the block moves from side to side through the day. It fluctuates with the season, with lying down, with exercise. And it responds to a steroid spray. A block that sits on one side, every day, and ignores four months of correct treatment is behaving like something that does not move: a deviated septum, a narrow valve, or both. That is the history of a structural obstruction, and it tells you what to look for when you examine him.

Why the others fail:
(A) A watery nose in the morning is a mucosal symptom, and he may well have some rhinitis alongside. But rhinitis alternates and responds to treatment. It does not explain a fixed left-sided block.
(C) Duration alone does not distinguish. Allergic rhinitis also lasts for years.
(D) No facial pressure argues against sinusitis, which is useful, but it does not tell you whether the remaining obstruction is lining or structure.

Keypoint: a one-sided block that never moves and never responds to a spray is structural until proven otherwise.

Reference: Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Clinical consensus statement: septoplasty with or without inferior turbinate reduction. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435. Clement PA, Gordts F; Standardisation Committee on Objective Assessment of the Nasal Airway, IRS, and ERS. Consensus report on acoustic rhinometry and rhinomanometry. Rhinology. 2005;43(3):169-179.

steps.title: Step 2/7: At the Bedside
steps.scenario: Before the endoscope, you want to localize the block with your hands. His history says the left side is fixed.
steps.question: Which maneuver pulls the cheek laterally to open the valve, and what does a negative result mean?

options.text: (A) Cottle maneuver; a negative result means the cause is not in the lateral nasal wall
(B) Valsalva maneuver; a negative result means the eustachian tube is blocked
(C) Modified Cottle maneuver; a negative result proves the septum is straight
(D) Toynbee maneuver; a negative result means the valve is collapsing

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The Cottle maneuver draws the cheek laterally, which pulls the lateral nasal wall outward and opens the valve angle. If he breathes better while you hold it, the valve is at least part of the problem. If nothing changes, the block is elsewhere: the septum, the turbinate, or further back. Either answer is useful, and a negative Cottle is often the more informative one because it takes the lateral wall off the list.

The modified Cottle is the more precise version: a cotton-tipped probe lifts the upper lateral cartilage from inside, or supports the ala, and he reports the change. It tells you which part of the lateral wall is at fault. His caudal septum is in the way on the left, so expect a weak response on that side.

Why the others fail:
(B) Valsalva tests the middle ear and eustachian tube. It does not examine the nasal valve.
(C) The modified Cottle uses a probe inside the nose, not traction on the cheek, and a negative result says nothing about the septum. It means the lateral wall is not the problem.
(D) Toynbee is swallowing against a pinched nose, another eustachian tube test.

Keypoint: pull the cheek; if it helps, the valve is at fault; if it does not, look at the septum.

Reference: Rhee JS, Poetker DM, Smith TL, et al. Laryngoscope. 2005;115(3):437-440. Cottle MH. Rhino-sphygmo-manometry: an aid in physical diagnosis. Int Rhinol. 1968;6:7-26.

steps.title: Step 3/7: The Endoscopy
steps.scenario:
You pass a rigid endoscope. The caudal septum is deviated to the left and sits off the anterior nasal spine in the left vestibule. Higher up, the dorsal septum also curves left. On both sides the angle between the septum and the upper lateral cartilage looks narrow. Both inferior turbinates are enlarged.

You spray a topical decongestant and look again ten minutes later. The turbinates have shrunk. The septum and the valve angle have not changed.
steps.media: Load image: Two endoscopic views of the left nasal cavity, before and after decongestant, unannotated: turbinate smaller in the second, caudal septum and valve angle unchanged. Caption: 'Before and after decongestant.'
steps.question: What has the endoscopy established?

options.text: (A) The block is mucosal; increase the steroid spray to double dose
(B) The block is turbinate hypertrophy; plan turbinate reduction alone
(C) Nothing can be concluded without a CT
(D) A structural block: caudal septal deviation with internal valve narrowing, neither of which moved with decongestant

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

The decongestant is the confirmation, and it belongs here, after the history and the Cottle have told you what to expect. It shrinks anything that is swollen and leaves anything that is fixed. His turbinates shrank, so they are part of the picture but not the part that blocks him. His caudal septum and his valve angle did not move, so they are.

The internal nasal valve is the narrowest point of the whole airway. Its walls are the septum medially, the caudal edge of the upper lateral cartilage superolaterally, the nasal floor below, and the head of the inferior turbinate behind. The angle between septum and upper lateral cartilage is normally 10 to 15 degrees, and because resistance rises steeply as that angle closes, a septum pushing in from the medial side or an upper lateral cartilage falling in from the lateral side is felt out of all proportion to its size. That is why his block is so much worse than the deviation looks.

Why the others fail:
(A) The lining already shrank with decongestant and the block stayed. More steroid treats lining that is not the problem.
(B) The turbinates are enlarged and will be reduced in the same operation, but they responded to decongestant. Reducing them alone leaves the septum and the valve, which is where he is blocked.
(C) The consensus statement is clear that CT may not accurately show the degree of septal deviation. You have just seen the deviation directly. CT would add nothing to the septal diagnosis, though it can be useful later for graft planning or if sinus disease is suspected.

Keypoint: history says structure, Cottle points to the valve, endoscopy with decongestant proves it; the septum and the valve angle are what did not move.

Reference: Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Clinical consensus statement: septoplasty with or without inferior turbinate reduction. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435. Kasperbauer JL, Kern EB. Nasal valve physiology: implications in nasal surgery. Otolaryngol Clin North Am. 1987;20(4):699-719. Rhee JS, Poetker DM, Smith TL, et al. Nasal valve surgery improves disease-specific quality of life. Laryngoscope. 2005;115(3):437-440.

steps.title: Step 4/7: Which Graft
steps.scenario: The caudal and high dorsal deviations are severe enough that a standard submucous resection will not straighten the dorsum or open the valves. You plan an open functional rhinoplasty and turbinate reduction.
steps.media: Load image: Intraoperative photograph, open approach, unannotated: bilateral spreader grafts sutured between the dorsal septum and the upper lateral cartilages. Caption: 'Spreader grafts.'
steps.question: Which graft straightens a high dorsal deviation and widens the internal valve angle at the same time?

options.text: (A) Columellar strut graft
(B) Alar batten graft
(C) Spreader grafts
(D) Caudal septal extension graft

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

Spreader grafts are strips of septal cartilage placed in a pocket between the dorsal septum and the upper lateral cartilage, then sutured through all three. They do two jobs. They splint the dorsal septum straight, and by holding the upper lateral cartilage away from the septum they widen the valve angle. They rebuild the T-shaped junction of the middle vault that a deviation has collapsed. They are the standard answer to a high dorsal deviation with valve narrowing.

A step further, for the surgeon rather than the student. Bilateral symmetric spreaders assume the septum is roughly central. When the septum itself is off center, as his caudal septum is, symmetric grafts widen the vault around the wrong midline. The alternative is to set a new midline with a caudal septal extension graft and splint the dorsal septum to it with a single extended spreader graft on the concave side. In the original series that corrected the dorsal deviation angle by 3.7 degrees and reduced nostril axis inclination by 11.7 degrees. It is the technique for a deviated cartilaginous vault when the midline has moved.

Why the others fail:
(A) A columellar strut supports the tip. It does not touch the dorsum or the internal valve.
(B) Alar battens reinforce the external valve, the ala and lateral crus, against collapse on inspiration. His problem is the internal valve.
(D) A caudal septal extension graft lengthens and supports the caudal septum and sets tip position. On its own it does nothing for the dorsum or the valve angle, though combined with a unilateral spreader it becomes the advanced answer above.

Keypoint: spreader grafts straighten the dorsal septum and open the internal valve; if the midline itself is displaced, build a new one first.

Reference: Rhee JS, Poetker DM, Smith TL, et al. Laryngoscope. 2005;115(3):437-440. Chen YY, Kim SA, Jang YJ. Centering a deviated nose by caudal septal extension graft and unilaterally extended spreader grafts. Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol. 2020;129(5):448-455. doi:10.1177/0003489419894617. Sheen JH. Spreader graft: a method of reconstructing the roof of the middle nasal vault following rhinoplasty. Plast Reconstr Surg. 1984;73(2):230-239.

steps.title: Step 5/7: The Turbinate
steps.scenario:
His inferior turbinates are enlarged. They shrank with decongestant in Step 3, so they are part mucosal, but they are still large and you will reduce them in the same operation.

You choose a submucosal technique with a microdebrider rather than removing the turbinate.
steps.media: Load image: Endoscopic view of submucosal inferior turbinate reduction with a microdebrider, mucosa preserved, unannotated. Caption: 'Submucosal reduction.'
steps.question: Which complication are you avoiding by preserving the mucosa?

options.text: (A) Cerebrospinal fluid leak
(B) Toxic shock syndrome
(C) Anosmia
(D) Empty nose syndrome

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

The inferior turbinate is not just a lump in the airway. Its mucosa warms and humidifies air and, more importantly, senses it: the feeling of breathing through the nose comes from receptors in that lining. Remove too much and you get a paradox. The airway is wide open on the scope, and the patient says he cannot breathe. That is empty nose syndrome, and there is no good treatment for it. So the turbinate is reduced from underneath, taking bone and submucosal tissue and leaving the surface intact. The consensus statement says the same: when the turbinate is reduced, the mucosa should be preserved.

Why the others fail:
(A) A CSF leak comes from the skull base, well above the inferior turbinate. It is not a turbinate surgery complication.
(B) Toxic shock is a complication of prolonged nasal packing, not of how much turbinate is removed. It is one of the reasons packing is avoided in Step 6.
(C) Smell lives on the olfactory cleft, high in the nose. The inferior turbinate does not carry it.

Keypoint: reduce the turbinate from underneath and keep the lining; a wide nose that cannot feel air is worse than the block you started with.

Reference: Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435. Coste A, Dessi P, Serrano E. Empty nose syndrome. Eur Ann Otorhinolaryngol Head Neck Dis. 2012;129(2):93-97.

steps.title: Step 6/7: Closing Without Packing
steps.scenario: The septum is straightened and grafted, the valves are open, both turbinates are reduced. You want the septal flaps to stay down, no hematoma, and no adhesion between the septum and the raw turbinate, without the misery of nasal packing.
steps.media: Load image: Endoscopic view at the end of the case showing a septal quilting suture, or a Doyle splint in place, unannotated. Caption: 'Closing.'
steps.question: How do you close?

options.text: (A) Tight bilateral nasal packing for five days
(B) A septal quilting suture, or soft silicone septal splints, and no packing
(C) Four weeks of high-dose systemic corticosteroid
(D) Leave the mucoperichondrial flaps open to drain

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

A septal hematoma forms when blood collects between the cartilage and the flap. The traditional answer was to pack both nostrils and press the flaps down from outside, which is painful, obstructs completely, and carries the small but real risk of toxic shock. The modern answer presses from inside. A running quilting suture through both flaps and the septum closes the dead space, and the consensus statement says it directly: quilting sutures can obviate the need for packing. Soft silicone splints do the same job, and they also keep the septum away from the raw surface of the reduced turbinate so the two cannot scar together. He goes home breathing through his nose.

Why the others fail:
(A) Packing works, but at a cost the patient does not need to pay: pain, complete obstruction, mouth breathing, and a toxic shock risk that rises with every day it stays in.
(C) Steroids do not close a dead space. A month of high-dose steroid after septal surgery adds harm and no benefit.
(D) Flaps left off the cartilage are exactly where the hematoma forms. Dead space is the enemy.

Keypoint: close the dead space from inside with a quilting suture or splints, and let him leave without packing.

Reference: Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435.

steps.title: Step 7/7: Six Months Later
steps.scenario:
He is back at six months. Breathing is much better and his NOSE score has fallen from 16 to 5. The dorsum is straight and both valves are open on endoscopy.

But on the basal view the columella has drifted back to the left, and the caudal septum is once again sitting to the left of the anterior nasal spine. At the first operation the caudal septum was straightened by scoring and repositioned, but it was not fixed to the spine.
steps.media: Load image: Basal view at six months, consented, unannotated: columella tilted left, caudal septum visible in the left vestibule. Caption: 'Six months.'
steps.question: Why did it come back, and what does a revision have to do differently?

options.text: (A) The turbinate regrew; reduce it again
(B) The spreader grafts were too short; add longer ones

(C) Cartilage memory pulled the scored caudal septum back. The revision must release it from the spine, reposition it onto the midline, suture it to the periosteum, and splint it with a bony batten or an extension graft
(D) Resect the dislocated caudal centimeter so there is nothing left to deviate

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

The caudal septum is the one part of the septum that scoring and repositioning alone will not hold. Cartilage remembers its shape, and a caudal end that has been bent straight without being anchored drifts back over months. Anterior deviations are the ones that recur after septoplasty, and this is why. The spreader grafts held the dorsum; nothing was holding the caudal end.

The revision does four things. Release the caudal septum from its false position on the spine. Reposition it onto the midline over the anterior nasal spine. Suture it down to the periosteum of the spine, so it is fixed and not merely placed. Then splint it, because a thin repositioned septum needs something rigid alongside it: a bony batten harvested from the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, which is the strongest option and has good outcome data for exactly this problem, or a caudal septal extension graft when the septum also needs length. Fixation plus splinting is what turns a repositioned septum into a stable one.

Why the others fail:
(A) The turbinate is not what you see in the vestibule. The block has moved back to the caudal septum, and reducing the turbinate again would leave it there.
(B) The dorsum is straight. The spreaders did their job. They sit in the middle vault and have no hold on the caudal septum.
(D) Resecting the caudal septum removes the tip's support. The tip drops, the columella retracts, and you trade a deviation for a saddle. The caudal strut is repositioned and reinforced, never resected.

Keypoint: a repositioned caudal septum without fixation and a splint will come back; fix it to the spine and give it a batten.

Reference: Han JK, Stringer SP, Rosenfeld RM, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;153(5):708-720. doi:10.1177/0194599815606435. Gubisch W. Twenty-five years experience with extracorporeal septoplasty. Facial Plast Surg. 2006;22(4):230-239. Chung YS, Seol JH, Choi JM, et al. How to resolve the caudal septal deviation? Clinical outcomes after septoplasty with bony batten grafting. Laryngoscope. 2014;124(8):1771-1776. Kim D, Nam SH, Al-harethy S, et al. Surgical outcomes of bony batten to correct caudal septal deviation in septoplasty. JAMA Facial Plast Surg. 2017;19(6):470-475.
